title: Bank chief risk officers are losing sleep over rogue AI agent threats
full_text:
For banks around the world, including Australia’s largest institutions, the threat of rogue artificial intelligence agents causing real-time system issues, or even financial chaos, has become very real.
Banks, which are heavily regulated, typically have cyber defences that are extremely difficult to penetrate. Even so, revelations over the past week about AI agents accessing Medicare data, and bots targeting a raft of other government websites, would have bank chief risk officers on high alert.
On Saturday AEST, OpenAI said it had paused training of its latest AI models to ramp up a review of agents going beyond stated tasks while trawling government and other websites.
That decision will provide some respite to government agencies and banks, but the underlying risks related to hacking activity by AI agents remain.
Already in March and April this year, the Reserve Bank of Australia and the prudential regulator separately cautioned financial institutions about the increased potential for cyber and security incidents associated with AI and high-capability models.
As far as we can tell, Australia’s largest banks are being proactive in terms of their efforts to ward off these threats. Commonwealth Bank and Westpac, for example, are using OpenAI’s Daybreak, which is adept at identifying cybersecurity vulnerabilities and is powered by the same advanced models as Anthropic’s Mythos.
CBA has a strategic partnership with OpenAI and is also a shareholder in Anthropic, which may list on the Nasdaq before the year’s end.
“Without effective guardrails and oversight, [generative and agentic AI ] could increase operational, legal, and reputational risks.”
Miriam Fernandez, S&P director of AI research and adoption
That comes as moves accelerate in the United States to expand a powerful industry group, dubbed the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure, which wants to address risks posed by AI. Last month, JPMorgan’s chief executive Jamie Dimon was actively seeking to draft more members into the group by personally contacting leaders of large and regional banks and technology companies.
And Australia’s policymakers have now also become acutely aware of the risks, following the Medicare incident. On Friday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese suggested a new global body with similar investigatory powers as the International Atomic Energy Agency was needed to govern AI.
For banks there is a real trade-off in this area as they seek to benefit from AI and agents – think operational efficiencies, cost reduction and more fulsome customer interactions – while balancing that against the protection of data and ensuring the robustness of financial systems.
The last thing any financial institution wants is a large-scale incident that puts at risk its systems, depositor funds or creates fear or contagion within the financial system. Just ask London-based Revolut, which has an Australian banking licence, and has recently been the subject of a more traditional human hacker-led data breach. That issue affected some 680 customers, believed to be those with cryptocurrency holdings.
Separately, a report by S&P Global earlier this month suggested that while AI could help to strengthen a bank’s risk management, it may also leave financial institutions vulnerable to threats around data security, reliability and accountability.
“Without effective guardrails and oversight, they [generative and agentic AI] could increase operational, legal, and reputational risks,” said the report authored by Miriam Fernandez, S&P’s director of AI research and adoption.
“Broader industry-level risks could also challenge financial stability, including due to cyber contagion, third-party concentration, and the potential for agentic systems to contribute to market volatility and herding.”
The report, based on a survey of 179 financial institutions across four regions including the Asia Pacific, found 67 per cent of respondents had a reliance on third-party providers. While that is not necessarily negative, the figure shows those banks and other players are exposed to further risks.
One of the most worrisome figures in the report, though, was that while 69 per cent of respondent institutions said they had AI governance frameworks, just 39 per cent of those included board-level oversight. Europe, the Middle East and Africa and North America were highlighted as having the most mature AI governance, while Latin America and the Asia Pacific lagged.
On a positive note, S&P’s report suggested if banks utilised AI to improve the management of credit risk and better engage with customers, that could boost the agency’s assessment of an institution’s creditworthiness.
“The uneven pace of adoption, governance maturity, and operational readiness suggests AI will increasingly contribute to the strengthening or weakening of [a financial institution’s] creditworthiness over the next several years,” it said.
“While successful AI adoption alone is unlikely to be a rating driver, it is likely to support creditworthiness over time if institutions are able to convert stronger sustained profitability into durable competitive advantage and more effective risk management than peers.”
The median financial institution surveyed by S&P expected AI-driven cost reductions of up to 4 per cent this year, accelerating to as much as 8 per cent by 2028.
Macquarie analysts reckon greater customer personalisation through AI could intensify competition for higher-margin products and low-cost deposits, leading banks to “more effectively target customers that are most likely to switch”.
But that won’t necessarily benefit their respective bottom lines. “Consistent with our AI paradox thesis, better execution does not necessarily translate into higher earnings if the benefits are ultimately competed away across the industry,” the Macquarie analysts said.
AI adoption presents vast opportunities for banks, but for now, the more pressing priority is to get ahead of the threats.
